title: Cache
body:
A small, fast memory between the [[CPU]] and [[Main memory]], holding copies of recently
used data. It exists for one reason: **main memory is much slower than the processor**, so
without it the CPU would spend most of its cycles waiting on the [[Bus]].

## Why it works

Programs are not random. They exhibit **locality of reference**, in two flavours:

- **Temporal locality**: an address used now will probably be used again soon (a loop
  counter, the top of the stack).
- **Spatial locality**: addresses near one just used will probably be used soon (walking an
  [[Array]], executing straight-line code).

Spatial locality is why cache moves data in **lines** or blocks of several words rather than
single bytes: fetching the neighbours is nearly free once the [[Main memory]] access has
been paid for.

## Hits, misses, and the sum that matters

A **hit** is finding the address in cache; a **miss** is not, and costs a main-memory access
on top. With hit rate $h$, the average access time is

$$t_{\text{avg}} = h \cdot t_{\text{cache}} + (1-h) \cdot t_{\text{memory}}$$

Because $t_\text{memory}$ is so much larger, hit rates need to be very high before the
average looks good; 95% still means one access in twenty pays full price. Real hit rates are
in the high nineties, which is why the whole scheme is worth the silicon.

## The memory hierarchy

Each level is bigger, slower, and cheaper per byte than the one above:

| Level | Rough size | Rough access |
|---|---|---|
| Registers | tens of bytes | 1 cycle |
| Cache (L1/L2/L3) | KB to MB | a few to tens of cycles |
| [[Main memory]] (RAM) | GB | hundreds of cycles |
| Disk / SSD | TB | millions of cycles |

The trick is the same at every level, and [[Virtual Memory]] in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] is
literally this idea one rung down: RAM caching the disk, with page faults playing the part
of misses.

## Coherence

Once there is more than one cache, they can disagree about the same address. A write in one
core's cache is invisible to another core reading its own copy, and [[Direct Memory Access]]
writes straight to memory behind every cache's back. Keeping them consistent is the **cache
coherence** problem, and it is the reason [[Synchronization]] primitives in
[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] need hardware support ([[TAS|test-and-set]]) rather than clever
ordinary code.
